samasa.vigraha: स्त्रीषु रत्नम् स्त्रीरत्नम्; स्त्रीरत्नं भूता, ताम्
samasa.type: karmadhāraya with भूत ‘being’, containing a saptamī tatpuruṣa (स्त्रीरत्न, of selection)
samasa.literal: who has become the jewel among women
samasa.alt: स्त्रीरत्न may also be read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, स्त्रीणां रत्नम्; the sense is the same.

samasa.sense: those to whom every treasure belongs by right

morph.note: Present ātmanepada of √मन्, fourth class (मन्य-): ‘we think, regard’. With two accusatives: त्वाम् (object) and स्त्रीरत्नभूताम् (what she is regarded as).
Nominative plural of the root-noun रत्नभुज् (j-final): the bare root with zero affix (kvip) as the final member of an upapada compound, like ‘-bhuj’ in भूभुज् ‘enjoyer of the earth, king’.
The pronoun सा resumes the predicate of the first line: ‘you, being such (a jewel)’. सा त्वम् is a common Purāṇic opening for a request.

mantras.anvaya: देवि, वयं लोके त्वां स्त्रीरत्नभूतां मन्यामहे। यतः वयं रत्नभुजः, (अतः) सा त्वम् अस्मान् उपागच्छ।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first sentence has a double accusative (त्वाम् … स्त्रीरत्नभूताम्). The second is an imperative with a causal clause (यतः …) giving the reason.
mantras.lit: We regard you, O Devī, as being the jewel among women in the world. Such as you are, come to us, since we are the enjoyers of jewels.
mantras.tr: We hold you, O Devī, to be the jewel among the women of the world. Come to us, then, for jewels are ours to enjoy.

comm.t: The argument of the message is now explicit: every jewel belongs to Śumbha, the Devī is the jewel among women, therefore she must come to him. Śumbha speaks of himself in the plural (वयम्), as a king.

The word रत्न has carried the whole speech from 5.109. The tradition reads the irony of the scene: the one he names a ‘jewel’ to be owned is the power by whom, in the narrator’s words of 5.116, the world itself is upheld.

samasa.literal: she whose outer eye-corners are restless
samasa.sense: a woman with lively, darting glances — a conventional epithet of beauty

morph.note: Imperative of √भज्. Its basic sense is ‘to share, resort to’; with a man as object, of a woman, it means to choose him, give oneself to him in marriage.
A bahuvrīhi ending in a body-part (अङ्ग) forms its feminine with -ī: चञ्चलापाङ्गी; the vocative shortens the ī: चञ्चलापाङ्गि.

mantras.anvaya: चञ्चलापाङ्गि, यतः त्वं वै रत्नभूता असि, (अतः) मां वा मम अनुजम् उरुविक्रमं निशुम्भं वा अपि भज।
mantras.anvaya_en: An imperative (भज) with two alternative objects joined by वा … वा अपि, and a causal clause (यतः …) at the end.
mantras.lit: Choose me, or else my younger brother Niśumbha of wide valour, O you of darting glances — since you are indeed a jewel.
mantras.tr: Take me, or my younger brother Niśumbha of mighty valour, O lady of the darting glance — for a jewel is what you are.

comm.t: The proposal itself: the Devī may choose either brother. The reason is the same as in 5.112 — she is a jewel, and jewels go to the brothers.

The offer of a choice between two husbands prepares the Devī’s answer: she will lay down one condition for either of them (5.120–121). The narrative leaves both brothers in the frame; both will meet her, but only in battle (chapters 9–10).

samasa.sense: the highest wealth and power there is

samasa.literal: having no balance (to be weighed against)

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (the genitive is subjective: ‘my taking (you)’)

samasa.vigraha: मम परिग्रहः मत्परिग्रहः; तस्य भावः मत्परिग्रहता, ताम्
samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa with the abstract suffix -ता
samasa.literal: the state of being my possession, my wife
samasa.alt: परिग्रह means both ‘taking, acceptance (in marriage)’ and ‘what is taken: wife, possession’. In मत्परिग्रहात् the act is meant, in मत्परिग्रहताम् the status; the same word was used of possessions in 5.98 (भ्रातुस्तव परिग्रहे).

morph.note: Future of प्र + √आप् (आप् + स्य → आप्स्य-), with the ātmanepada ending -से where classical usage has the parasmaipada प्राप्स्यसि. Such voice changes are frequent in the epic and Purāṇic language.

The abstract suffix -ता (tal) makes a feminine noun of state from the compound: ‘my-consort-ness’. With a verb of motion (व्रज) the accusative names the condition one passes into: ‘go to the state of …’, i.e. ‘become …’.
Absolutive of the tenth-class root √लोच् with two prefixes: the causative -ay- is dropped before -य (lyap). ‘Having weighed (it) well’.

mantras.anvaya: मत्परिग्रहात् (त्वम्) अतुलं परमैश्वर्यं प्राप्स्यसे। एतत् बुद्ध्या समालोच्य मत्परिग्रहतां व्रज।
mantras.anvaya_en: A promise in the future (प्राप्स्यसे), then an imperative (व्रज) preceded by an absolutive (समालोच्य) with its object एतत्.
mantras.lit: You will obtain supreme, matchless sovereignty from being taken by me. Having considered this well with your understanding, go to the state of being my consort.
mantras.tr: As my wife you will gain a sovereignty beyond compare. Weigh this well in your mind, and become my consort.”
mantras.tr_note: The closing quotation mark ends the message quoted in Śumbha’s words (from 5.108).

comm.t: The message ends with an inducement and a command: marriage to Śumbha will give the Devī matchless power; she should think it over and consent.

The offer reverses the truth the text has already stated: the gods’ hymn has just praised her as the power present in all beings (5.14–80), and the narrator will call her the one by whom the world is upheld (5.116). Śumbha offers her what is already hers.
A modern reading: the appeal to ‘consider it with your intelligence’ invites calculation. The Devī will answer not with a calculation but with a vow made long before (5.119–120).

comm.t: Medhas, the seer, takes up the narration again after the messenger’s speech (5.106–114) and tells King Suratha how the Devī replied.

sandhi.type: vowel sandhi inside a compound (savarṇa-dīrgha); visarga kept
sandhi.note: a + a → ā. The visarga of अन्तः stays before the sibilant s inside the compound.
ā + i → e; the final m of इदम् becomes anusvāra before धार्यते (मोऽनुस्वारः, 8.3.23).

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (two attributes of one subject); inside it अन्तःस्मिता = अन्तः स्मिता ‘smiling within’ (the adverb अन्तः with the participle स्मिता)
samasa.sense: outwardly serious, with a smile kept inside
samasa.alt: Also read as a bahuvrīhi, गम्भीरम् अन्तः स्मितं यस्याः सा ‘she whose inner smile was deep’. Both keep the contrast of a grave face and a hidden smile; the karmadhāraya keeps the simpler parts.

morph.note: Perfect of √गै ‘sing’: reduplicated ज- (g → j) + गौ. Used here, as often in the Purāṇas, simply for ‘spoke, declared’.
Passive of the causative धारय- (√धृ ‘to hold’): the causative -ay- is dropped before the passive -ya-: धार्-य-ते, ‘is upheld’.
Past participle of √वच् with samprasāraṇa (va → u): उक्त. In the passive sense of a verb of speaking it means ‘the one spoken to’.

mantras.anvaya: इति उक्ता सा देवी, दुर्गा भगवती भद्रा, यया इदं जगत् धार्यते, तदा गम्भीरान्तःस्मिता जगौ।
mantras.anvaya_en: The subject देवी has three appositive names and a relative clause (यया … धार्यते); the main verb is जगौ with the predicate adjective गम्भीरान्तःस्मिता.
mantras.lit: Thus addressed, the Devī then, grave and smiling within, spoke — Durgā, the Blessed, the Auspicious, by whom this world is upheld.
mantras.tr: So addressed, the Devī — Durgā, the Blessed, the Auspicious, by whom this world is upheld — grave of face yet smiling inwardly, gave her answer.
mantras.tr_note: The appositive names are brought forward next to देवी.

comm.t: The narrator introduces the Devī’s reply. The contrast is marked: she is grave, but smiles within. The second line steps out of the scene to remind the hearer who is being asked to marry Śumbha — the one by whom the world is upheld.

The hidden smile is read as the key to her reply: what she says will be courteous and literally true, while its meaning is the opposite of surrender. The name Durgā, ‘hard to approach’, is apt at the very moment an asura proposes to take her.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has two of the names given here: 190, दुर्गा, and 279, भगवती. The coincidence of names reflects a shared Śākta vocabulary; the two texts are separate works.
